analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey records AI use across finance and insurance at 40.0%, up from 36.8% in the prior period, making it one of the more consistently measured adoption figures among major sectors. That figure covers the broader finance and insurance grouping rather than depository banking alone, but it signals that firms in this space are adopting AI at a rate that outpaces many other industries.

Banking is unusual in that AI governance did not begin with the recent generative AI wave. Credit scoring and fraud detection models have operated for decades, and the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, already requires banks to validate, document, and oversee quantitative models, a framework that regulators have since extended to machine learning and AI applications. This means banking is the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade, giving examiners an existing supervisory vocabulary to apply to newer tools.

The open-model landscape for financial applications can be tracked through resources such as the financial models catalogue on this site, which monitors the most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub across licence type, download volume, and release date. That catalogue reflects the growing supply of models tuned for financial text, a supply that feeds both vendor products and internal bank development efforts.

On the risk and regulatory side, the sourced points note that Treasury has mapped the risk surface for AI in financial services across uses, opportunities, and risks, framing the US supervisory conversation at the federal level. What the actual Treasury page retrieved by this site's pipeline contains is a sanctions action unrelated to AI, so the specific findings of that report are not available to summarize here, and readers should consult the Treasury document directly for its substance.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy AI in a banking context, the practical takeaway from these sources is that the governance infrastructure already exists and will be applied. SR 11-7 compliance is not optional, and any model used in credit, anti-money-laundering, or similar decisions carries validation obligations regardless of whether it is described as traditional statistical modeling or generative AI. The Evident AI Banking Index, noted in the sourced points as scoring major global banks across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency metrics, offers one public benchmark for understanding where peer institutions stand on AI maturity, though its detailed findings are not reproduced in the material available here.
